lead: Distributorless ignition removes the rotating distributor and gives each coil its own job. In the common waste-spark form, one coil serves a pair of cylinders and fires both plugs together: one spark occurs near the end of compression, the useful one, and the other occurs in the exhaust stroke and is wasted. Direct ignition goes further: one coil per cylinder, mounted on or near the plug, fires only on compression. The engine control unit (ECU) decides timing from crank and cam position. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic, so treat it as an advanced extension of Chapter 2.3.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for ECU switching and the coil driver, plus basic crank and cam sensor ideas from Unit 3.

blocks.text: Waste-spark ignition uses one coil for two cylinders whose pistons rise and fall together but whose strokes are opposite. In a four-cylinder engine with firing order 1-3-4-2, the pairs are 1&4 and 2&3. The ECU charges the coil primary, interrupts it at the calculated angle, and the secondary sends high voltage to both plugs. One plug is near the end of compression and lights the mixture. The other is in exhaust and its spark is wasted, though it still loads the coil. Each coil fires twice in the 720° cycle, which is two crank revolutions. Coil 1&4 fires at cylinder 1 compression and 360° later at cylinder 4 compression. Coil 2&3 fires at 180° and 540°. The figure shows this order. Waste spark needs no distributor cap, rotor or long high-voltage cables, so it is cheap and common on small engines.

sections.h3: Direct ignition: one coil per cylinder

blocks.text: Direct ignition gives every cylinder its own coil, mounted on the plug (coil-on-plug) or close to it (coil-near-plug). The ECU fires that coil only on the compression stroke. A crank sensor and a trigger wheel give speed and crank angle within one revolution. A trigger wheel is a toothed disc whose teeth pass a sensor; a missing tooth or a special tooth marks a reference. The crank alone cannot separate compression from exhaust because the two revolutions look identical. A cam sensor turns at half crank speed and adds the phase. With both signals the ECU knows the 720° position and can fire each coil once per cycle. This is why direct ignition needs a cam sensor for true sequential operation. The high-voltage path is short, so radio interference and cable leakage fall. Timing is more accurate because there is no rotor gap or mechanical advance to wear.

The service picture changes. There is no rotor to burn or cap contact to erode, and no distributor shaft play to upset timing. A misfire on one cylinder points to that cylinder's coil, plug or short high-voltage boot; a paired misfire on a waste-spark engine points to the shared coil. The ECU can cut fuel to a cylinder and watch crank speed, or measure coil current, to identify a dead coil. Replacement coils are often smart coils with built-in igniters, triggered by a low-voltage signal. Keep the plug gap and heat range correct: a wide gap raises the voltage demand and can cause flashover inside a worn coil boot. For the driver circuit inside the ECU see Unit 4; for sensor physics see Unit 3.

figure.caption: Each bar marks the firing window of one cylinder, drawn 60° wide only for visibility; the instant of the spark is the start of the bar. Coil 1&4 sparks at 0° (cylinder 1) and 360° (cylinder 4); coil 2&3 sparks at 180° (cylinder 3) and 540° (cylinder 2).

spec.aria: Timeline of one 720 degree cycle showing coil 1 and 4 firing at 0 and 360 degrees and coil 2 and 3 firing at 180 and 540 degrees, in firing order 1-3-4-2.

examples.question: A 4-cylinder engine with firing order 1-3-4-2 runs at 4000 rpm on a waste-spark system with coils paired 1&4 and 2&3. Find the sparks per second per coil and the crank angle of each spark in the 720° cycle.
steps: A 4-stroke cycle needs 2 revolutions, so total sparks per second = 66.67 × 2 = 133.3.
Each of the two coils fires half the sparks: 133.3 ÷ 2 = 66.7 sparks per second per coil.
Cylinder 1 fires at 0°, cylinder 3 at 180°, cylinder 4 at 360° and cylinder 2 at 540°. Coil 1&4 sparks at 0° and 360°; coil 2&3 sparks at 180° and 540°.
examples.answer: Each coil sparks 66.7 times per second, the engine produces 133.3 sparks per second, the 720° cycle lasts 30 ms, and the sparks occur at 0° (cylinder 1), 180° (cylinder 3), 360° (cylinder 4) and 540° (cylinder 2).
examples.check:
rpm = 4000
rev_s = rpm / 60
total = rev_s * 2
per_coil = total / 2
cycle_ms = 2 / rev_s * 1000
print(round(per_coil, 2))
print(round(total, 2))
print(round(cycle_ms, 2))
for a in [0, 180, 360, 540]:
    print(a)

traps: Forgetting the 720° cycle: a crank sensor alone cannot separate compression from exhaust.
Thinking a waste-spark coil fires once per revolution; a paired coil fires twice in 720°.
Pairing cylinders by neighbouring numbers instead of by equal piston position and firing order.
Ignoring the wasted spark when calculating coil energy: both plugs load the same secondary.
Calling coil-near-plug the same as coil-on-plug; one has a short high-voltage cable.

quiz.a: Both plugs of a paired coil fire together; one spark is on compression, one on exhaust.

quiz.q: Why does direct ignition need a cam sensor?
quiz.a: Crank gives angle but not which revolution is compression; cam gives phase for 720°.

quiz.q: A 4-cylinder waste-spark engine runs at 6000 rpm. Find sparks per second per coil.
quiz.a: 6000 rpm = 100 rev/s; total 200 sparks/s; each coil 100 sparks/s.

quiz.q: Compare waste spark and coil-on-plug for timing accuracy and cost.
quiz.a: Coil-on-plug fires only on compression and allows individual cylinder timing, at the cost of one coil per cylinder plus a cam phase sensor; waste spark uses half the coils but delivers one wasted spark per pair and cannot trim timing cylinder by cylinder.

quiz.q: Name the two forms of distributorless ignition and one common synonym for the family.
quiz.a: The two forms are waste-spark (paired coil) and direct (coil-per-cylinder). The family as a whole is also called distributorless ignition system (DIS) or electronic ignition (EI).

quiz.q: What does a missing tooth on a trigger wheel provide?
quiz.a: A crank reference mark so the ECU can count angle from a known position.

quiz.q: Firing order 1-3-4-2, coil 1&4 sparks at 0°. Give the next three spark angles and cylinders.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern engines use coil-on-plug with ion-current sensing, where the spark plug also measures combustion. Higher coil voltage and smart igniters help lean-burn and high-compression engines. Search next for coil-on-plug, ion current sensing and ignition coil driver.
